newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to make fresh bid to improve beef safety.
newsitem.headline: EU to make fresh bid to improve beef safety.

text.p: A fresh bid will be made this month to tighten controls on mad cow disease by banning risky cattle tissues, a European Commission spokesman said on Friday.

He was responding to a warning on Thursday from British Farm Minister Jack Cunningham who said Britain may ban beef imports unless the European Union agreed by July 22 to apply the same tough safety standards as in Britain.

"We welcome the fact that they support the Commission approach of tightening up BSE controls. We are working actively to try and find an EU solution," Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said.

Kiely said the EU's executive would resubmit a proposal to ban specified risk material from cattle and sheep -- brains, eyes, spinal cord and spleen -- to the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee of senior member state officials.
"There's a good chance it will be made before the next meeting of EU farm ministers (June 23-250)," he said.
If there was a weighted majority in favour, the Commission would then impose the ban. If not it could then be sent to a meeting of EU farm ministers on July 22.
Kiely declined to speculate what the EU would do if Britain introduced a unilateral beef import ban.

"It's a hypothetical situation," he said, adding that unilateral action taken in previous years by German states against imports of British cattle and beef were either transposed into EU measures or scrapped.

The EU banned British beef and beef products more than a year ago when the previous Conservative government admitted a possible link between bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease), a deadly brain disease, and its human equivalent, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

In December, farm ministers rejected a proposal to ban risky cattle parts, arguing it was an unnecessary economic burden as their countries were virtually free of BSE and scrapie, a similar brain-wasting disease in sheep.
Infected meat and bonemeal, containing the risky organs and mixed into cattle and sheep feed, is believed to be the main cause of BSE.

But recent EU inspections have shown that not all countries have been respecting food safety rules to eliminate BSE and that the disease may be far more widespread than officially recognised because farmers and veterinarians are failing to report it.
Britain imports most of its beef from Ireland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, trade sources said.
Only Germany does not remove spinal cords and other risky parts from cattle and sheep.
